name: Brand, Positioning and Voice
description: What a brand is, brand strategy, positioning, audiences, architecture and naming, visual and verbal identity, governance, brand in product, partnerships, metrics, reputation, change and accessible channel voice.

cards.subject: Brand
says: is the sum of perceptions people hold about an organisation or product
exists in people's minds whether or not the company manages it
is shaped by every experience, not only by marketing
cards.use: need a word for what customers believe and feel about the company
not: is the same thing as the logo

cards.subject: Brand identity
says: is what the organisation deliberately puts out to express the brand
covers the name, visuals and language the company controls
cards.use: need to list the assets the company controls to express itself
not: is how audiences actually perceive the company today

cards.subject: Brand image
says: is the perception audiences hold at a given point in time
is learned through research rather than designed
can differ from the identity the company intended
cards.use: want to learn what customers really think of the company
not: is the set of approved design files

cards.subject: Brand reputation
says: is the accumulated judgement of reliability built over a long period
is earned by repeatedly delivering on promises
changes slowly because it rests on many past interactions
cards.use: need to explain why one bad week does not define how the market sees a long-trusted firm
not: can be rebuilt with one campaign

cards.subject: Brand equity
says: is the extra commercial value a name adds beyond the product itself
shows up as price premium, preference or easier launches
cards.use: want to explain why people pay more for the same product under a trusted name
not: is the book value of the company's buildings

cards.subject: Brand touchpoint
says: is any point where a person encounters the brand
includes invoices, support calls and packaging as well as adverts
cards.use: need to map every place customers meet the company
not: covers paid advertising only

cards.subject: Brand experience
says: is the cumulative impression left by interactions across touchpoints
is built by what people do and feel, not only by what they read
cards.use: need to judge how the whole relationship feels rather than a single message
not: is limited to the visual design of the website

cards.subject: Brand loyalty
says: is repeat preference for a brand even when alternatives are available
is measured by behaviour such as repurchase and retention
cards.use: want to know whether customers keep choosing the brand over time
not: is the same as awareness

cards.subject: Brand trust
says: grows when the brand does what it says again and again
is the confidence that the brand will act in the customer's interest
is damaged quickly by a broken promise
cards.use: need to explain why customers accept the company's claims without checking them
not: can be bought through a larger media budget

cards.subject: Brand purpose
says: states why the organisation exists beyond making money
answers the question why at the base of the strategy
cards.use: need to explain why the company exists beyond profit
not: lists the financial targets for next year

cards.subject: Brand vision
says: describes the future the brand wants to help bring about
is long-term and aspirational
cards.use: need to describe the future state the brand is working toward
not: describes the daily activities of the team

cards.subject: Brand mission
says: states what the organisation does and for whom today
is the present-tense route toward the vision
cards.use: need a plain statement of what the organisation does and for whom
not: is a distant ideal that may never be reached

cards.subject: Brand values
says: guide behaviour and decisions inside the company
show up in the choices made when two good options conflict
cards.use: need a basis for deciding between two options that both look reasonable
not: are slogans chosen for the front page of the website

cards.subject: Brand promise
says: states what customers can count on every time
is judged by whether the experience delivers it
cards.use: need a commitment that customers can hold the company to
not: is a discount offered to new customers

cards.subject: Brand personality
says: describes the brand as a set of human traits
guides how the brand behaves and speaks
cards.use: need to decide whether the brand should feel warm, bold or precise
not: is the legal name of the company

cards.subject: Brand strategy pyramid
says: layers purpose, values, promise and personality so each supports the next
gives one page showing how the foundation connects to the expression
cards.use: want one page that shows how the brand's purpose connects to its personality
not: ranks competitors by market share

cards.subject: Brand essence
says: distils the brand into a few words capturing its core
is an internal reference point rather than a public line
cards.use: need the shortest internal statement of what the brand stands for
not: is the tagline printed on adverts

cards.subject: Brand archetype
says: casts the brand as a recognisable character such as the sage or the rebel
borrows from archetypal patterns found in stories
cards.use: want a familiar character model to keep personality coherent
not: is a market segment

cards.subject: Brand platform
says: bundles the strategic elements into one reference that teams build from
sits upstream of campaigns and guidelines
cards.use: need one foundation document before briefing agencies and writers
not: is the software used to publish posts

cards.subject: Positioning
says: defines the place a brand claims in the target audience's mind relative to alternatives
chooses what to be known for and what to leave out
cards.use: need to decide how the brand should be seen next to competitors
not: is the physical location of the shops

cards.subject: Positioning statement
says: names the target, frame of reference, key benefit and reason to believe
is an internal sentence for aligning teams, not published verbatim
cards.use: need a short internal brief that aligns teams on where the brand sits
not: is the public slogan shown beside the logo

cards.subject: Differentiation
says: makes the offer different in a way the audience values
fails when the difference does not matter to buyers
cards.use: want a reason for customers to choose you over a similar option
not: means being the cheapest in the category

cards.subject: Frame of reference
says: names the category or alternatives the audience compares you with
changes which competitors the audience considers
cards.use: need to choose which category the brand will be judged against
not: is the camera angle used in photography

cards.subject: Point of parity
says: is an attribute the audience expects because category rivals all have it
is needed to be considered yet earns no preference by itself
cards.use: need to check that table-stakes features are covered before stressing uniqueness
not: is the single feature that only your brand offers

cards.subject: Point of difference
says: is a benefit that is relevant, distinctive and believable
gives buyers a reason to prefer the brand
cards.use: need one benefit that rivals cannot credibly claim
not: is a feature all category brands share

cards.subject: Reason to believe
says: is the proof that backs up a brand claim
can be a feature, data point, certification or demonstration
cards.use: hear a benefit claim and need evidence that makes it credible
not: is the emotional benefit itself

cards.subject: Value proposition
says: states the specific value delivered to a customer segment and why it beats alternatives
is customer-facing and tied to an offer
cards.use: need to explain to a buyer what they get and why it is better
not: is an internal list of the company's beliefs

cards.subject: Perceptual map
says: plots brands on two axes that matter to buyers
reveals crowded areas and open space in a market
cards.use: need to see where competitors cluster and where room is open
not: lists the stores on a city map

cards.subject: Competitive audit
says: reviews how rivals present their name, claims and visuals
finds claims that everyone in the category already makes
cards.use: need to learn what competitors already say before choosing a message
not: measures the financial results of rivals

cards.subject: Generic positioning
says: claims qualities every competitor claims, such as quality and service
leaves buyers no reason to choose the brand
cards.use: notice that a rival's tagline could replace yours and nobody would notice
not: is the strongest basis for differentiation

cards.subject: Repositioning
says: changes the place the brand holds in audience minds
needs changed product or proof, not only new words
cards.use: find the brand is seen in the wrong category and need to shift that perception
not: is a change of office address

cards.subject: Target audience
says: is the specific group a brand focuses its effort on
is narrower than everybody
cards.use: need to decide who a message is mainly for
not: is every person who could ever see the brand

cards.subject: Market segmentation
says: splits a market into groups with shared needs or traits
lets effort concentrate on groups worth serving
cards.use: need to divide a broad market into groups before choosing who to serve
not: combines all customers into a single average profile

cards.subject: Demographic segment
says: groups people by facts such as age, income and location
cards.use: need to group customers by facts that can be read from a census-style record
not: groups people by attitudes and lifestyle

cards.subject: Psychographic segment
says: groups people by attitudes, values and lifestyle
explains motives that demographics cannot show
cards.use: need to group customers by what they believe and care about
not: groups people by purchase frequency

cards.subject: Behavioural segment
says: groups people by actions such as usage rate, purchase frequency and loyalty
cards.use: need to group customers by what they actually do with the product
not: groups people by age and income

cards.subject: Persona
says: is a fictional but research-based profile of a typical segment member
makes audience needs concrete for writers and designers
cards.use: need to help a team picture who they are writing and designing for
not: is a real customer's confidential record

cards.subject: Customer insight
says: is a non-obvious truth about motivation that a brand can act on
differs from a raw observation or data point
cards.use: need an unexpected truth about why people behave as they do to build a message on
not: is a count of website visits

cards.subject: Stakeholder
says: is anyone who affects or is affected by the brand, such as staff, investors and regulators
makes the audience wider than customers alone
cards.use: need to remember that brand decisions also matter to staff and regulators
not: is only a person who holds company shares

cards.subject: Customer journey map
says: lays out the stages from first awareness to repeat purchase and advocacy
shows where the brand experience is weak
cards.use: need to see where people drop off between first contact and repeat purchase
not: lists the delivery routes of a courier

cards.subject: Jobs to be done
says: frames the audience by the progress they want to make rather than who they are
explains why different demographics buy for the same reason
cards.use: find that demographics do not predict who buys and need a better lens
not: groups buyers strictly by age band

cards.subject: Brand architecture
says: defines how the brands in a portfolio relate to each other
decides which brand name appears where
cards.use: need rules for how a company's brands and sub-brands relate
not: is the design of the company's office building

cards.subject: Branded house
says: uses one master brand across all products
lets each product build on shared awareness
cards.use: want every product to build recognition for one name
not: gives every product a fully independent name

cards.subject: House of brands
says: gives each product its own independent brand
keeps trouble in one brand from damaging the others
cards.use: want to serve very different audiences without mixing their reputations
not: puts the parent name on every product

cards.subject: Endorsed brand
says: keeps a product brand but adds the parent name as a guarantee
sits between the branded house and the house of brands
cards.use: need product names to stand alone yet borrow the parent's credibility
not: hides all trace of the parent

cards.subject: Sub-brand
says: extends the master brand with its own name and some distinct traits
stays visibly tied to the parent
cards.use: need a named offer for a niche that still clearly belongs to the master brand
not: has no visible link to the parent

cards.subject: Brand portfolio review
says: prunes overlapping brands that compete for the same audience
cuts the cost of maintaining many names
cards.use: find several of our brands target the same buyers and need to simplify
not: adds a new brand for each new feature

cards.subject: Naming brief
says: sets objectives, audience, tone and constraints before names are generated
stops the process from drifting to personal taste
cards.use: need to align stakeholders on criteria before brainstorming names
not: lists the names already chosen

cards.subject: Descriptive name
says: says what the company or product does
is easy to understand but harder to trademark and own
cards.use: need a name that explains the offer at first read
not: is a coined word with no prior meaning

cards.subject: Invented name
says: is a coined word with no prior meaning
is easier to protect legally but must be taught to the audience
cards.use: want a distinctive name that is likely to be available as a trademark and domain
not: tells people exactly what the product does

cards.subject: Evocative name
says: suggests a quality or feeling without describing the product
borrows meaning from a real word or image
cards.use: want a name that hints at the experience rather than the function
not: is built from the initials of a longer name

cards.subject: Name clearance
says: checks a candidate name for legal conflicts, domain availability and cultural problems
happens before a name is adopted
cards.use: have a shortlisted name and need to check it before committing
not: is the creative brainstorm that produces names

cards.subject: Hybrid architecture
says: mixes branded-house and house-of-brands rules by product line
needs explicit criteria for when each applies
cards.use: find that a single rule does not fit acquired brands and organic products alike
not: applies one master brand to every product without exception

cards.subject: Logo
says: is a graphic mark or wordmark that identifies the brand
is one asset within the visual identity
cards.use: need a recognisable mark to sign off documents and products
not: is the entire brand

cards.subject: Wordmark
says: sets the brand name in distinctive lettering without a symbol
relies on typography to be recognised
cards.use: need a logo made only of the name in a distinctive typeface
not: is a symbol with no letters

cards.subject: Brand colour palette
says: defines primary and secondary colours with exact values
keeps colour recognisable across print and screen
cards.use: need approved colours with exact codes for every medium
not: lets each designer choose any shade

cards.subject: Typography
says: sets the typefaces, sizes and hierarchy used for text
gives written material a recognisable look
cards.use: need to choose fonts and heading hierarchy for all materials
not: selects the colours of the logo

cards.subject: Imagery style
says: sets rules for the subject, composition and treatment of photography and illustration
keeps pictures recognisably from the same brand
cards.use: find that photos from different suppliers look unrelated
not: fixes the wording of headlines

cards.subject: Iconography
says: defines a family of icons with shared stroke weight and corner style
keeps small symbols visually consistent in interfaces
cards.use: find icons from several sources clash in the product interface
not: covers photography direction

cards.subject: Design tokens
says: store design decisions such as colour and spacing as named values
let one change flow through web and app code
cards.use: need to update a brand colour once and have every platform follow
not: are paid vouchers redeemed in the shop

cards.subject: Design system
says: combines components, patterns and tokens into reusable building blocks
speeds up building consistent interfaces
cards.use: need teams to build interfaces from shared parts instead of redrawing them
not: is a single colour chart

cards.subject: Brand guidelines
says: document how to apply the identity assets and voice correctly
give staff and agencies rules and examples
cards.use: need a reference that tells anyone how to use the logo, colour and tone
not: are legally binding trademark registrations

cards.subject: Clear space
says: is the minimum empty margin kept around a logo
stops other elements crowding the mark
cards.use: need a rule so text never sits too close to the logo
not: is the smallest size a logo may be printed

cards.subject: Logo lockup
says: fixes the arrangement of mark, wordmark and tagline as a single unit
has approved horizontal and stacked versions
cards.use: need an approved arrangement of symbol and name to fit narrow and wide layouts
not: is the legal registration of the logo

cards.subject: Motion identity
says: defines how elements animate, including timing and easing
gives movement a recognisable character
cards.use: need rules for how interface elements move so animation feels like the brand
not: is the set of fonts for video captions

cards.subject: Brand voice
says: is the consistent personality expressed in words
stays the same across channels and over time
cards.use: need to describe how the brand sounds in all writing
not: changes entirely for each situation

cards.subject: Tone of voice
says: adapts the voice to the situation and the reader's emotional state
is gentler in an apology than in a promotion
cards.use: need to adjust wording between an error message and a celebration
not: is the fixed personality that never varies

cards.subject: Style guide
says: sets writing rules such as spelling, capitalisation, punctuation and terminology
settles small choices so writers do not decide each time
cards.use: need to settle whether to write email or e-mail everywhere
not: specifies the logo size and colours

cards.subject: Messaging hierarchy
says: orders messages from the core promise down to supporting proof points
tells writers which message leads
cards.use: need to decide which message leads a page and which ones support it
not: lists the departments in the organisation chart

cards.subject: Message house
says: shows an umbrella message with supporting pillars and proof beneath
presents the hierarchy as a visual that teams can share
cards.use: want a one-page picture of the main message, its pillars and evidence
not: is the building where the marketing team sits

cards.subject: Tagline
says: is a short memorable phrase that sums up the brand and sits with the logo
is meant to last for years
cards.use: need a lasting phrase that appears alongside the logo
not: is rewritten for every campaign

cards.subject: Campaign line
says: is tied to one campaign and expected to be replaced
is more time-limited than a tagline
cards.use: need a phrase for a seasonal promotion
not: is the permanent line printed under the logo

cards.subject: Boilerplate
says: is a standard about-us paragraph reused at the end of press releases
keeps the company description consistent everywhere
cards.use: need approved wording to close every press release
not: is an advertising slogan

cards.subject: Terminology list
says: fixes the approved names for products, features and concepts
stops one feature being called three things
cards.use: notice the docs, app and sales deck use different names for the same feature
not: sets the colour values for the brand

cards.subject: Voice chart
says: maps each voice trait to what it means and what it does not mean, with examples
helps writers apply a trait without overdoing it
cards.use: need writers to apply friendly without becoming silly or casual in serious moments
not: lists the monthly posting dates

cards.subject: Brand consistency
says: means audiences meet the same identity and message at every touchpoint
builds recognition through repeated exposure
cards.use: want people to recognise the brand wherever they meet it
not: means using identical wording in every situation

cards.subject: Brand governance
says: assigns owners, approval paths and rules to protect the brand
balances control with the speed teams need
cards.use: need clear ownership of who decides brand questions
not: is a government regulation on branding

cards.subject: Brand asset library
says: holds approved logos, templates and images in one place
stops people using outdated files
cards.use: find staff are copying old logos from email attachments
not: reviews the quality of campaign copy

cards.subject: Approval workflow
says: routes new material for sign-off before publication
should be lighter for low-risk items
cards.use: need a checkpoint before external materials go out
not: measures brand awareness

cards.subject: Brand audit
says: reviews how consistently the brand appears across channels and materials
finds off-brand items for correction
cards.use: need a view of how consistently the brand shows up across channels
not: measures competitors' advertising spend

cards.subject: Brand champion network
says: places advocates in each team to promote and check brand use locally
relies on volunteers embedded in each team rather than a central body
cards.use: need people in every region to spot misuse and coach colleagues
not: is the central approval committee

cards.subject: Brand council
says: is a cross-functional group that decides brand questions and exceptions
resolves conflicts between consistency and local needs
cards.use: need a body to rule on requests that break the guidelines
not: is a group of external customers who test products

cards.subject: Local adaptation
says: lets regional teams adapt the brand within defined limits
balances consistency against local relevance
cards.use: need to localise a campaign without breaking the core identity
not: bans any translation of brand materials

cards.subject: Brand drift
says: is gradual departure from guidelines through many small unnoticed deviations
is fixed by audit and clear ownership rather than blame
cards.use: notice that materials made over two years look unlike each other
not: is a sudden planned redesign

cards.subject: Microcopy
says: is the small interface text such as button labels and hints
shapes how the brand voice feels in the product
cards.use: need to write the words on buttons, tooltips and form fields
not: is the long-form text in a white paper

cards.subject: Error message
says: states what happened and what to do next in the brand voice
avoids blame and jokes when the user is stuck
cards.use: need wording for a screen that appears when a payment fails
not: should be written as a marketing slogan

cards.subject: Empty state
says: is the screen shown before content exists, a chance to guide in the brand voice
points the user to a first useful action
cards.use: need a screen for a new account that has no data yet
not: is a broken page with no explanation

cards.subject: Onboarding flow
says: is the first-use sequence that sets the product's impression
teaches value early in the brand's tone
cards.use: need to design the first minutes a new user spends in the product
not: is the exit survey for departing users

cards.subject: Transactional email
says: is a system message such as a receipt or password reset
reaches nearly every customer and is a brand touchpoint
cards.use: find that receipts and reset emails look unlike the rest of the brand
not: is a bulk promotional newsletter

cards.subject: Dark pattern
says: tricks users into actions they did not intend
erodes trust and damages the brand
cards.use: spot a cancellation flow that hides the exit button
not: is a theme designed for night-time reading

cards.subject: Say-do gap
says: is the distance between what the brand says and what the product does
is a main driver of customer cynicism
cards.use: find the adverts promise speed but the product is slow
not: is the gap between two release dates

cards.subject: Employer brand
says: is the reputation of the organisation as a place to work
is shaped by current employees' real experiences
cards.use: struggle to attract applicants who fit the culture
not: is the company's consumer advertising

cards.subject: Employee value proposition
says: states what an employee gets in return for their contribution
is the core promise of the employer brand
cards.use: need a clear statement of why people should join and stay
not: is the customer value proposition

cards.subject: Employee advocacy
says: has staff share the brand story in their own voice and networks
depends on voluntary, authentic sharing rather than scripts
cards.use: want employees to share the company news without sounding scripted
not: means paying staff to post identical text

cards.subject: Co-branding
says: joins two brands on one offer so each lends the other credibility
needs agreed rules on logo use and approvals
cards.use: plan an offer carrying both our name and a partner's
not: hides the maker's name from the buyer

cards.subject: White-labelling
says: supplies a product that another company sells under its own brand
hides the maker's name from the end customer
cards.use: need to sell a product built by another firm under our own name
not: shows both brands equally on the offer

cards.subject: Private label
says: is a product made for a retailer and sold under the retailer's own brand
lets the retailer control price and presentation
cards.use: are a retailer wanting a store-brand version of a common product
not: is a product sold under two equal brands

cards.subject: Brand licensing
says: lets another party use a brand name on products in return for fees
depends on quality control by the owner
cards.use: want other manufacturers to make goods carrying our brand
not: transfers ownership of the brand to the buyer

cards.subject: Ingredient branding
says: promotes a component brand inside another company's product
makes the component a visible reason to buy
cards.use: are a component maker who wants buyers to ask for our part by name
not: hides the supplier from the buyer

cards.subject: Sponsorship
says: associates the brand with an event or team to borrow its audience and meaning
needs a fit between sponsor and property
cards.use: want to borrow the passion of a sports audience for the brand
not: is a paid search advertisement

cards.subject: Influencer partnership
says: uses a creator's audience trust to carry the message
must be disclosed as paid where required
cards.use: plan to work with a creator whose followers match our audience
not: is an employee sharing company news

cards.subject: Unaided awareness
says: is recall when asked about a category with no prompt
is a stronger signal than recognition from a list
cards.use: want to know which brands people name first when no list is shown
not: is recognition after seeing a list of names

cards.subject: Aided awareness
says: is recognition when the name is shown or read from a list
is higher than unaided awareness for the same brand
cards.use: want to know whether people recognise the name when prompted
not: is recall with no prompt

cards.subject: Brand consideration
says: measures the share of the audience who would put the brand on a shortlist
sits between awareness and purchase
cards.use: need to know how many people would consider us when buying
not: counts only people who already bought

cards.subject: Brand awareness
says: measures whether people recognise or recall the brand
is the first step before consideration
cards.use: want to know how many people have even heard of the brand
not: measures the number of repeat purchases

cards.subject: Net Promoter Score
says: subtracts the share of detractors from the share of promoters
is based on one likelihood-to-recommend question
cards.use: need a single recommend-question score tracked over time
not: averages star ratings on a shop page

cards.subject: Brand sentiment
says: measures whether mentions are positive, neutral or negative
can be tracked automatically on social channels
cards.use: want to see whether the tone of online conversation about us is improving
not: counts how many people follow the page

cards.subject: Share of voice
says: is the brand's portion of total category advertising or mentions
shows how loudly the brand competes with rivals
cards.use: need to compare our visibility with competitors in the same category
not: is a measure of sales revenue

cards.subject: Share of search
says: is the brand's proportion of category search queries
is used as a proxy for mental availability
cards.use: want a cheap signal of interest compared with competitors that updates continuously
not: is the brand's portion of paid adverts

cards.subject: Brand tracking study
says: repeats the same survey on the same questions over time
shows movement in awareness and perception
cards.use: need to see how perceptions change quarter by quarter
not: is a one-off creative test

cards.subject: Brand lift study
says: compares exposed and unexposed groups to estimate a campaign's effect
isolates the effect of a specific campaign
cards.use: need to estimate how much a campaign moved awareness or intent
not: tracks the same measures every quarter without a control group

cards.subject: Vanity metric
says: looks impressive but does not link to a business outcome
includes raw follower counts
cards.use: hear a report celebrate follower numbers with no link to sales or consideration
not: is the most reliable measure of brand health

cards.subject: Crisis communication plan
says: names spokespeople, approval routes and first responses before an incident
speeds up the first hours of a response
cards.use: want to be ready to respond quickly if something goes wrong
not: is written after the crisis ends

cards.subject: Holding statement
says: is a brief first response that acknowledges the situation while facts are gathered
buys time without inventing details
cards.use: need to say something within minutes before the facts are known
not: is the final detailed report on the cause

cards.subject: Social listening
says: monitors mentions across channels to catch issues early
feeds sentiment and trend insight
cards.use: want early warning of a complaint spreading online
not: measures how many people saw an advert

cards.subject: Brand safety
says: keeps ads away from harmful or unsuitable content
protects the brand from guilt by association
cards.use: need to prevent adverts from appearing next to unsuitable content
not: protects the product from physical damage

cards.subject: Trademark
says: is a sign that identifies the source of goods or services and can be registered
protects names and logos from confusing copies
cards.use: need legal protection for a name or logo
not: protects an original written article

cards.subject: Copyright
says: protects original works such as photographs and written text
arises on creation of the work in many countries
cards.use: need to know whether we can reuse a photographer's picture
not: protects a brand name for a product category

cards.subject: Genericide
says: happens when a brand name becomes the common word for the whole category
weakens the owner's trademark protection
cards.use: worry that people now use our brand name as the word for the product type
not: makes the name easier to defend legally

cards.subject: Greenwashing
says: exaggerates environmental claims
risks regulatory action and lost trust
cards.use: hear a campaign make broad green claims with no evidence
not: is a certified sustainability audit

cards.subject: Reputation recovery
says: rebuilds trust through changed behaviour as well as statements
takes longer than the original incident
cards.use: are rebuilding trust after a serious failure
not: is complete once an apology is published

cards.subject: Brand extension
says: uses an existing brand name on a new product category
borrows awareness to cut launch costs
cards.use: want to launch a product in a new category under the existing name
not: adds a new flavour to an existing product

cards.subject: Line extension
says: adds variants such as sizes or flavours within the same category
has less brand risk than moving to a new category
cards.use: want to add a new size and flavour under the same brand
not: moves the brand into an unrelated category

cards.subject: Brand dilution
says: weakens what a brand stands for by stretching it too far
happens when extensions have little in common with the core
cards.use: find that new products under the name confuse what the brand is known for
not: strengthens the brand's meaning

cards.subject: Rebranding
says: changes the name, identity or positioning of a brand substantially
needs a clear reason and a managed transition
cards.use: merge two companies and need a new name and identity
not: only fixes a typo in a logo file

cards.subject: Brand refresh
says: updates visual elements while keeping the name and positioning
modernises without breaking recognition
cards.use: want a modern look while keeping the name and positioning
not: changes the company's name and positioning

cards.subject: Brand fit test
says: checks whether a new product matches what the brand stands for
looks at both customer perception and brand meaning
cards.use: are deciding whether a new product suits the brand
not: tests whether the logo fits on packaging

cards.subject: Redirect plan
says: maps old web addresses to new ones so links and search ranking survive a rename
is a technical step in rebranding
cards.use: are renaming the company and changing the domain
not: lists the new logo files

cards.subject: Social media voice
says: adapts the brand voice to a conversational platform while keeping the personality
replies to people directly
cards.use: need to write posts that sound like the brand but fit a conversational feed
not: uses a formal press release style for every post

cards.subject: Channel playbook
says: sets tone, formats and posting norms for one channel
lets teams adapt the voice without losing consistency
cards.use: need rules on how the brand behaves on each platform
not: is the company-wide logo rulebook

cards.subject: Content pillar
says: is a recurring theme that content is organised around
keeps output focused on topics the audience values
cards.use: find our posts jump between unrelated topics
not: is a fixed daily posting time

cards.subject: Social response policy
says: decides when to reply, escalate or ignore comments
keeps responses consistent between moderators
cards.use: need to know how to handle a hostile comment
not: lists the hashtags for a campaign

cards.subject: Colour contrast ratio
says: measures the luminance difference between text and background
has minimum values in accessibility guidelines
cards.use: need to check whether brand colours make text readable
not: measures how bright the colour looks in print

cards.subject: Colour independence
says: means information is never conveyed by colour alone
helps people who cannot distinguish certain colours
cards.use: find an error is shown only by a red outline
not: requires all designs to be black and white

cards.subject: Alt text
says: describes an image for people who use screen readers
should convey the image's purpose
cards.use: need to make an image meaningful to a screen-reader user
not: is the caption printed beneath the picture

cards.subject: Plain language
says: uses short common words and direct sentences
reduces effort for readers with different reading levels
cards.use: find our instructions are full of jargon
not: means removing all personality from copy

cards.subject: Inclusive language
says: avoids terms that exclude or stereotype groups
widens who feels addressed by the brand
cards.use: want copy that does not exclude any group of readers
not: is a ban on all descriptive words

cards.subject: Trend-jacking
says: ties brand content to a trending topic
is risky when it is off-brand or insensitive
cards.use: consider joining a viral conversation unrelated to our brand
not: is a scheduled evergreen post

qa.q: Which statement best separates a brand from a logo?
qa.right: A brand is the sum of perceptions people hold; a logo is one asset that identifies it
wrong: A brand is the registered version of a logo
A logo is what customers feel and a brand is the drawing
They are two words for the same asset
qa.why: The logo is a visual mark inside the identity; the brand lives in people's minds.

qa.q: Which strategy element answers why the organisation exists beyond making money?
qa.right: Purpose
qa.why: Purpose is the foundation layer that states why the organisation exists.

qa.q: A founder says: 'Our brand is whatever we say it is.' What is the flaw in this view?
qa.right: Audiences form their own perceptions from every experience, whatever the company says
wrong: Brands can only be defined by lawyers
A brand cannot be changed once created
qa.why: Brand is perception, shaped by experience, not a declaration.

qa.q: Which pairing of brand strategy elements is in the right order from foundation to expression?
qa.right: Purpose, values, promise, personality
qa.why: Strategy layers build from why, through beliefs and commitment, to character.

qa.q: What does a positioning statement usually contain?
qa.right: Target, frame of reference, key benefit and reason to believe
wrong: Colour codes, fonts and logo sizes
A list of every product feature
qa.why: These elements make a positioning statement a usable internal brief.

qa.q: A team's positioning says 'high quality and great service'. Every competitor says the same. What is the best next step?
qa.right: Find a benefit that is relevant, distinctive and believable, and back it with proof
wrong: Add more adjectives to the claim
Drop the claim and use a new logo
qa.why: Differentiation needs a distinct, credible difference, not a louder generic claim.

qa.q: Which of these is a point of parity for a bank?
qa.right: Safe storage of customers' money
wrong: A unique payments feature no rival offers
The colour of the app icon
qa.why: Parity points are table stakes expected in the category.

qa.q: Which sentence is a reason to believe?
qa.right: Independent lab tests confirm it lasts twice as long as the previous model
qa.why: A reason to believe is proof, such as data or certification.

qa.q: Which segmentation groups customers by what they do with the product?
qa.right: Behavioural
qa.why: Behavioural segments use actions such as usage and loyalty.

qa.q: A company groups buyers by values and lifestyle. What kind of segmentation is this?
qa.right: Psychographic
qa.why: Psychographic segments use attitudes, interests and values.

qa.q: Why do teams write personas?
qa.right: To make segment needs concrete for people who write and design
wrong: To list every customer by name
To set the price of products
qa.why: A persona is a research-based profile used for empathy and focus.

qa.q: A company sells chocolate bars and a sportswear line to very different audiences and wants a failure in one not to harm the other. Which architecture fits?
qa.right: House of brands
qa.why: A house of brands keeps reputations independent.

qa.q: A software firm launches a new product and wants it to build on the awareness of its existing name. Which architecture fits?
qa.right: Branded house
wrong: Independent brand with no link to the parent
qa.why: A branded house leverages the master brand's awareness.

qa.q: A new brand name is a coined word with no meaning in any language. What is the main trade-off?
qa.right: Easy to protect and own, but it must be taught to the audience
wrong: Hard to trademark but instantly understood
Describes the product but can't be pronounced
Impossible to use as a domain name
qa.why: Invented names are distinctive but carry no inherent meaning.

qa.q: Before adopting a shortlisted name, what should a team do?
qa.right: Check legal conflicts, domain availability and meaning in key languages
wrong: Print it on packaging to see how it looks
Register social handles without any checks
qa.why: Name clearance prevents costly legal and cultural problems.

qa.q: Which is the best definition of clear space for a logo?
qa.right: A minimum empty margin around the mark that other elements must not enter
wrong: The smallest print size of the logo
A white version of the logo
qa.why: Clear space protects legibility and recognition of the mark.

qa.q: What is the benefit of design tokens?
qa.right: A brand decision such as a colour can be changed once and flow to every platform
qa.why: Tokens store design decisions as named values shared by code and design.

qa.q: A designer wants to use a slightly different blue for a new landing page because it looks nicer. Which guideline governs the choice?
qa.right: The brand colour palette with its exact values
qa.why: Colour values come from the palette; the style guide covers writing.

qa.q: Which pair correctly distinguishes voice from tone?
qa.right: Voice is the consistent personality; tone adapts to the situation
wrong: Voice adapts to the situation; tone never changes
Voice is for print; tone is for digital
qa.why: Voice is constant; tone flexes with context and emotion.

qa.q: A brand voice is described as 'warm, plain and confident, never jokey'. Which rewrite of 'Your payment was declined, you silly goose' fits best?
qa.right: Your payment didn't go through. Please check your card details and try again.
wrong: OOPS!!! Payment failed lol, try again!
Dear customer, we regret to inform you that your transaction cannot be completed.
qa.why: The rewrite is warm, plain and helpful without jokes or stiffness.

qa.q: The style guide says to use sentence case in headings. Which heading follows it?
qa.right: How to reset your password
qa.why: Sentence case capitalises only the first word and proper nouns.

qa.q: Which tool tells writers which message leads and which messages support it?
qa.right: Messaging hierarchy
qa.why: The hierarchy orders core promise and supporting proof points.

qa.q: What is the difference between a tagline and a campaign line?
qa.right: A tagline is long-lived; a campaign line belongs to one campaign
wrong: A tagline is spoken; a campaign line is printed
A tagline is for B2B; a campaign line for B2C
qa.why: Taglines are meant to last; campaign lines are time-limited.

qa.q: Which problem does a terminology list solve?
qa.right: The same feature being called different names across docs, app and sales
wrong: Logos appearing in the wrong colour
qa.why: A terminology list fixes approved names for products and concepts.

qa.q: Three teams each created slightly different logos and slides over two years. What is this called?
qa.right: Brand drift
qa.why: Drift is gradual deviation through small unnoticed changes.

qa.q: What is the most effective first fix for staff using outdated logos from old emails?
qa.right: Provide one approved asset library and retire old files
wrong: Send a stricter warning email each month
qa.why: A single source of truth stops outdated files circulating.

qa.q: A regional team asks to adapt a campaign image to local culture. What principle applies?
qa.right: Allow adaptation within defined limits that protect the core identity
wrong: Let regions create whatever they want
Ask the region to use only English
qa.why: Local adaptation balances consistency with relevance.

qa.q: Which situation best justifies a brand council?
qa.right: Requests to break the guidelines keep arriving and need consistent rulings
wrong: A single logo file needs resizing
A typo is found in a social post
The CEO asks for the date of the launch
qa.why: A council rules on exceptions and conflicts across the business.

qa.q: An app's error message reads 'LOL! Oops, you broke it!' when a payment fails. What is the problem?
qa.right: Humour and blame are inappropriate when the user is blocked
wrong: It follows the voice chart exactly
qa.why: Tone should adapt: helpful and calm when the user is stuck.

qa.q: A cancellation flow hides the 'cancel' button under several screens. How does this affect the brand?
qa.right: It is a dark pattern that erodes trust
wrong: It has no effect on perception
qa.why: Manipulative flows contradict brand promises and harm trust.

qa.q: The adverts promise 'instant answers' but support takes days. What is this gap called?
qa.right: Say-do gap
qa.why: The gap between promise and delivery damages trust.

qa.q: Which best describes employer brand?
qa.right: The organisation's reputation as a place to work
wrong: The company's logo on job adverts
The legal name of the employer
qa.why: It is shaped by real employee experience.

qa.q: A phone-case maker's products sell under a retailer's own label, with no maker name shown. This is
qa.right: White-labelling or private label
qa.why: The maker is hidden and the retailer's brand is shown.

qa.q: A chip maker wants buyers of laptops to ask for its processor by name. Which approach fits?
qa.right: Ingredient branding
qa.why: Ingredient branding makes a component a visible reason to buy.

qa.q: Two brands launch a joint product with both logos shown. What should be agreed first?
qa.right: Rules for logo use, approvals and quality
qa.why: Co-branding needs clear shared rules.

qa.q: Which metric measures whether people name the brand without any prompt?
qa.right: Unaided awareness
qa.why: Unaided awareness is spontaneous recall.

qa.q: A report says the brand has 200,000 followers. What question shows whether this is a vanity metric?
qa.right: Does it connect to consideration, preference or sales?
wrong: Is the font on the chart correct?
qa.why: Metrics matter if they link to outcomes.

qa.q: How is Net Promoter Score calculated?
qa.right: Percentage of promoters minus percentage of detractors
qa.why: NPS subtracts detractors from promoters.

qa.q: Which metric compares a brand's portion of category advertising or mentions with rivals?
qa.right: Share of voice
qa.why: Share of voice shows relative visibility.

qa.q: Why does a brand lift study use an unexposed group?
qa.right: To estimate the effect that the campaign itself caused
qa.why: The control group isolates campaign impact.

qa.q: A negative story about a product starts spreading online. What should the crisis plan produce first?
qa.right: A holding statement that acknowledges the situation while facts are gathered
wrong: A full report on the cause
A deletion of all critical comments
qa.why: A holding statement buys time without inventing details.

qa.q: A company publishes a long apology but does not change the practice that caused the harm. What is likely?
qa.right: Trust does not recover because behaviour did not change
wrong: The brand gains a stronger position
qa.why: Recovery needs changed behaviour as well as statements.

qa.q: Which legal right protects a brand name for a category of goods?
qa.right: Trademark
qa.why: Trademarks protect signs that identify the source of goods.

qa.q: A designer downloads a stock photo licensed for web use only. May the team print it on a billboard?
qa.right: Not without checking whether the licence covers print
wrong: Yes, anything online is free to use
qa.why: Licences limit where and how an image may be used.

qa.q: People use one company's brand name as the everyday word for every product of that type, and the owner worries about its mark. This is
qa.right: Genericide
qa.why: When a name becomes the word for the category, protection weakens.

qa.q: A cereal brand adds a new flavour. What is this?
qa.right: Line extension
wrong: Brand extension into a new category
qa.why: A new variant within the same category is a line extension.

qa.q: A premium watch brand launches budget phones under its name and its core customers stop seeing it as luxury. What happened?
qa.right: Brand dilution
qa.why: Stretching too far weakens what the brand stands for.

qa.q: Which describes a brand refresh rather than a rebrand?
qa.right: A modernised logo and palette with the same name and positioning
wrong: A new name and new positioning
A merger with a new company name
A move into a new market category
qa.why: A refresh keeps name and positioning.

qa.q: A company changes its domain name during a rebrand. What helps keep search ranking and inbound links?
qa.right: Redirects from old addresses to the new ones
wrong: Keeping both sites live with different content
qa.why: Redirects carry links and ranking to the new address.

qa.q: Which colour use fails the principle of colour independence?
qa.right: Showing form errors only with a red outline
wrong: Showing a red outline plus an icon and text
Using colour and underlines for links
Labelling chart lines directly as well as with colour
qa.why: Information should never depend on colour alone.

qa.q: What does alt text do?
qa.right: Describes an image for people who use screen readers
wrong: Adds a caption under a picture
qa.why: Alt text conveys the purpose of an image to those who cannot see it.

qa.q: A social media manager wants to join a trending topic that is unrelated to the brand and slightly sensitive. What is the best judgement?
qa.right: Skip it; trend-jacking off-brand or sensitive topics risks harm
wrong: Join and ask followers to share
qa.why: Brand voice and sensitivity matter more than short-term reach.

qa.q: Which action keeps a brand voice consistent across several social channels?
qa.right: A channel playbook that adapts tone but keeps the personality
wrong: Posting identical text on every channel
Letting each moderator choose a personality
qa.why: Playbooks set norms per channel under a common voice.

qa.q: A hostile comment appears on a post. Which tool decides whether to reply, escalate or ignore?
qa.right: Social response policy
qa.why: A response policy gives moderators consistent rules.

qa.q: A product manager wants to launch a new category under the current brand. Which check comes first?
qa.right: Brand fit: does the product match what the brand stands for?
qa.why: Fit with brand meaning predicts extension success.

qa.q: A company's sales deck, product docs and website each use different names for the same feature. Which fix is most direct?
qa.right: Create and enforce a terminology list
qa.why: A terminology list fixes approved names.

qa.q: An acquired company keeps a strong separate name in one market but is folded under the parent elsewhere. Which concept explains the mix?
qa.right: Hybrid architecture
qa.why: Different rules apply by line or market under a hybrid.

qa.q: A survey shows high aided awareness but low consideration. What is the likely lesson?
qa.right: People know the name but do not see a reason to choose it
wrong: The logo needs a new colour
Awareness is too low to measure
qa.why: Awareness without consideration signals a positioning or relevance gap.
